gap_fill: The guide gives the mechanism only, not a pixel-level algorithm. Temporal gap-filling is one of three key algorithm enhancements, aimed at persistent data gaps (p.2), and the night branch uses both temporal and spatial gap-filling to improve coverage (p.10). VNP46A2 ships Gap_Filled_DNB_BRDF-Corrected_NTL (description 'Gap Filled BRDF corrected DNB Radiance') beside the unfilled DNB_BRDF-Corrected_NTL, with the same encoding (Table 8 p.16; App. B p.44); the product LongName is 'VIIRS/NPP Gap-Filled Lunar BRDF-Adjusted Nighttime Lights Daily L3 Global 15 arc-second Linear Lat Lon Grid' (p.43). How it works (p.24, paraphrased): when the temporal gap-filling routine is called, the date of the latest high-quality main-algorithm retrieval is reported in a separate SDS layer (the layer is not named there; Latest_High_Quality_Retrieval matches by name and by the Fig. 4F/5F panels). If an outlier is still detected after temporal filling, the algorithm 'defaults to a monthly climatology' built from the most recent moonless high-QA values. Filled values therefore come from earlier nights by design, and the flags are meant to let users judge whether a filled value is recent. Purpose: fewer persistent gaps from nighttime clouds, snow and ephemeral artifacts such as aurora (pp.24-25). Not stated: the temporal search window, the spatial method, the exact rule for which pixels get filled, and whether DNB_BRDF-Corrected_NTL itself is ever filled (the separate filled layer implies it is not; inference). QA mismatch: p.24 says gap-filling is reported in the mandatory QA flags (the table number is missing), but Collection 2 Table 9 (pp.16-17) has no gap-filled code; the Fig. 4E/5E legends (2015 and 2013 scenes) show older classes Main Algorithm / Temporal Gap-Filling / Outlier Removal / Fill Value / Water Pixel (pp.24-25). The example VNP46A2.A2024100 lists an unexplained prior-day input VNP46A2_DB.A2024099 at version .001 (p.43). Monthly and yearly composites fill aurora-contaminated pixels with gap-filled values (p.6), and composite quality code 2 means gap filled from historical data (Table 12, p.23).
latest_high_quality_retrieval: Encoding: uint8; units 'Number of days' (Table 8 p.16; 'Number of Days \n' in App. B p.44); fill 255; valid 0-254; scale_factor 1.0; offset 0.0 (Table 8 p.16; App. B pp.44-45). Table 8 description 'Latest high quality BRDF corrected DNB radiance retrieval' (p.16); App. B long_name 'The Latest High Quality BRDF Corrected DNB Radiance Retrieval' (p.44); Section 5.2 lists it as the latest high-quality retrieval (number of days) (p.15). Meaning (p.24, paraphrased): when temporal gap-filling is used, the latest high-quality date observed by the main algorithm is reported in a separate SDS layer, so users can judge whether a gap-filled value is recent. The Fig. 4F/5F panel 'Temporal Gap Filling (Latest Date Observed)' uses a 0 / 7 / >=16 Days colour scale (pp.24-25). Internal tension: the prose speaks of a date, but the layer is a uint8 count of days. Not stated: the day the count is measured from, what 0 means (for example, that tonight's own retrieval was high quality), what is stored when no filling happened, and what is stored after the monthly-climatology fallback. Reading it as the age in days of the value in the gap-filled layer is an interpretation (inference).
date_convention: Filename field 'A2018001' is the 'Julian Date of Acquisition (A-YYYYDDD)' (p.6): a literal 'A', the 4-digit year and the 3-digit day of year. 'Julian date' here means day of year, not a Julian Day Number: the Fig. 4/5 captions write 'DOY 2015-091' and 'DOY 2013-080' (pp.24-25), and every appendix example maps that way. VNP46A2.A2024100.h10v04 has RangeBeginningDate = RangeEndingDate = 2024-04-09, StartTime 2024-04-09 00:00:00.000 and EndTime 2024-04-09 23:59:59.000 (pp.43-44). VNP46A1.A2023100 covers 2023-04-10 00:00:00 to 23:59:59, with PGE_EndTime '2023-04-10 23:59:59.000000Z' (pp.39-40). The production stamp YYYYDDDHHMMSS decodes the same way: 2024065214519 matches ProductionTime 2024-03-05 21:45:19 (pp.39-40) and 2024147200718 matches 2024-05-26 20:07:18 (pp.43-44). Monthly and yearly files carry the first day of the period: VNP46A3.A2012183 starts 2012-07-01 (p.46) and VNP46A4.A2021001 starts 2021-01-01 (p.54). Other filename fields: product short name, hXXvYY tile, '.002' collection version, production time and '.h5' (pp.6-7). Not stated in words: whether DDD is a UTC or a local day, or which date a post-midnight local pass is filed under. Evidence for a UTC calendar day (inference): the 'Z' suffix on the VNP46A1 PGE_EndTime (p.39); the VNP46A2 file for day D takes the same-day VNP46A1 file as input (p.43); and the VNP46A1.A2023100.h10v04 inputs are granules stamped A2023100 .0536, .0542, .0718, .0724 and .0900 (p.39). Under standard VIIRS L1 naming (outside knowledge) those are UTC start times, so post-midnight local passes over 80-70°W are filed under that same date. Ian (arithmetic): A2022271 = 2022-09-28 (landfall about 19:05 UTC) and A2022272 = 2022-09-29, which should hold the first post-landfall night under the UTC-day reading; confirm with VNP46A1 UTC_Time.
overpass_time: Not stated in the guide. A full-text search finds no local overpass or equator-crossing time for S-NPP or NOAA-20. Related facts: VNP46A2 has no time layer (List 2 p.15; Table 8 p.16). Per-pixel time exists only in VNP46A1 UTC_Time: float32, 'Decimal hours', fill -999.9, valid 0-24, scale 1.0 (Table 5 p.12), long_name 'View Time (UTC)' (App. A p.43). Gridding keeps, per cell, a high-quality observation least affected by cloud and off-nadir viewing from the available 6-min granules (p.7), so the pass used can differ between pixels and nights (inference); VNP46A1's Granule layer records the selected granule (Table 5 p.13). Figure 3 names 'Geometry, Overpass Time' as inputs to the Miller lunar irradiance model but gives no value (p.9). The Pitahaya field experiment ran at 02:00 local time (p.27); that is the experiment's time, not a stated overpass time. The example VNP46A1 h10v04 tile drew on granules stamped 05:36 to 09:00 on its own date (p.39; UTC under standard VIIRS naming, outside knowledge). Outside knowledge, not from the guide, to verify with UTC_Time: S-NPP crosses the equator on its night pass near 01:30 local mean solar time. Solar time at Lee County (about 82°W) is about UTC-5.5 h, so expect passes roughly 06-08 UTC (about 02-04 EDT), not 01:30 EDT.

tile_grid.naming: hXXvYY, the 'Tile Identifier (horizontalXXverticalYY)' in file names (p.7). Figure 2 numbers h00-h35 left to right (west to east) and v00-v17 top to bottom (north to south) (p.7); its caption gives 460 non-overlapping land tiles of approximately 10°×10° (p.8). Tiles are 2400 × 2400 (App. B phony_dim_0 = phony_dim_1 = 2400, p.44) at 15 arc-second resolution (pp.2, 6; DataResolution, p.43); 2400 × 15 arc-seconds = exactly 10°, and pixel_deg = 1/240° (arithmetic). Example bounds: h10v04 has W -80, E -70, N 50, S 40 with matching GRing points (pp.39-40, 43-44); h10v05 has N 40 (p.50) and S 30 (p.54). TileID '61010004' = h10v04 (pp.39, 43) and '61010005' = h10v05 (p.50). Derived, not stated: tile hXXvYY spans lon -180+10·XX to -170+10·XX and lat 80-10·YY to 90-10·YY, so h = floor((lon+180)/10) and v = floor((90-lat)/10). Lee County (26.3-26.8°N, 81.6-82.3°W) lies wholly in h09v06 (90-80°W, 20-30°N).

caveats: Page convention: every page number here, including the integer page fields, is the number printed at the bottom of the page, as used by the guide's own contents page, Reader A and agent-docs.md. PDF page index = printed page + 6 (printed p.1 = PDF p.7; front matter ii-vi = PDF pp.2-6). Reader B cited PDF indices; its numbers point to the same pages.

Gap-filled radiance hides outages by design. It carries the latest earlier high-quality value or a monthly climatology of recent moonless high-quality values (p.24), so a cloudy or poor-quality night after landfall can show pre-storm lights (inference). Use DNB_BRDF-Corrected_NTL with Mandatory_Quality_Flag = 0 for event nights. The guide implies, but never says in words, that this layer holds only the current night's retrieval. Latest_High_Quality_Retrieval shows how old a filled value is.

Collection 2 Mandatory_Quality_Flag has one good code, 0. The others are 1 = outlier, potential cloud contamination or other issues; 2 = solar zenith 102-108°; 3 = lunar eclipse; 4 = aurora; 5 = glint; 255 = fill (Table 9 pp.16-17; App. B Description p.45). No code means gap-filled, although p.24 says gap-filling is reported in the QA flags and the Fig. 4E/5E legends show older classes (pp.24-25); trust Table 9 and the in-file Description. The daily outlier test is not described, so whether a real sudden blackout can be flagged 1 is unknown.

Fill and twilight: Table 5 footnote 1 says fill values can arise from bad-quality data or from solar zenith < 102°, the code's nighttime cut-off (p.13). The footnote is attached to VNP46A1's DNB_At_Sensor_Radiance; carrying it over to VNP46A2 is inference, consistent with MQF 2 covering 102-108° (p.17). Not stated: whether cloudy pixels in DNB_BRDF-Corrected_NTL hold a value or the fill value, so build the clear mask from the flags, not from fill (inference).

Clouds: retrievals use the VIIRS cloud mask (VCM/VNP35; pp.3, 8). Per-pixel cloud confidence is QF_Cloud_Mask bits 6-7 (Table 6 p.14), which VNP46A2 adopts by reference (Table 8 footnote 3, p.16). Nighttime cloud masking is difficult, for example over snow (Fig. 4 caption, p.24). Expect many cloudy, MQF 1 or fill pixels on the first nights after a hurricane (inference).

Water and coast: the Fig. 4E/5E legend lumps 'Fill Value / Water Pixel' together (pp.24-25), but Table 9 does not say water is fill. QF_Cloud_Mask bits 1-3 give 011 = Sea Water and 101 = Coastal (p.14). This matters for Lee County's coast and barrier islands (inference).

View angle: artificial lights show a strong angular effect, and nadir radiance over dense urban centres can be much higher than off-nadir (p.6). VNP46A2 has no view-angle layer (List 2 p.15); Sensor_Zenith is only in VNP46A1 (Table 5 p.11). The composites split near-nadir (VZA 0-20°) and off-nadir (VZA 40-60°) (Table 11 pp.19-22). Night-to-night geometry changes can mimic or hide dimming (inference).

Moon: VNP46A2 removes moonlight with a lunar BRDF model and per-pixel lunar irradiance (Eqs. 1-3, pp.3-5); moonlight is present for about 50% of the lunar cycle (Fig. 1 caption, p.4). On moon-free nights the algorithm sets θm = 10° and Em = 0.26 nW·m−2 (unit as printed; the layer itself is in nWatts·cm−2) (p.5). Lunar zenith > 108° means a moonless night (Fig. 7 caption, p.28). DNB_Lunar_Irradiance counts × 0.1 = nWatts·cm−2 (Table 8 p.16; App. B p.44). The residual moonlight error of the daily product is not given.

Sensitivity targets (Table 14 pp.26-27), threshold / breakthrough / goal: Lmin 3.0 / 0.5 / 0.25 nW·cm−2·sr−1; robustness L0 ±3.0 / ±0.10 / ±0.05; stray-light error 0.45 / 0.25 / <0.1; spatial resolution 742 m / 500 m / ≤200 m (each ±5%); temporal resolution monthly / daily / hourly; geolocation uncertainty 133 / 50 / 20 m. The moon-free Pitahaya test puts VNP46A2 within the breakthrough Lmin, quoting 0.43 nW·cm−2·sr−1, and 16.95% more sensitive than TOA (p.28); in-situ reference data are scarce (p.27). Dim rural pixels sit near this floor (inference).

Footprint vs grid: the DNB ground footprint is a nearly constant ~742 m (p.7), coarser than the 15-arc-second cell (about 463 m north-south and 415 m east-west at 26.5°N; arithmetic). Neighbouring pixels are not independent and county edges blur; the guide does not discuss aggregation to boundaries (inference).

Vegetation correction is not applied in Collection 1 or 2 (p.10), although Eq. 1 contains the canopy term P↑(θv) (p.3). Storm defoliation could raise observed radiance and offset a real outage (inference). Nighttime AOD is extrapolated from daytime AOD at 0.550 µm, with NCEP water vapour, ozone and surface pressure (p.3); no accuracy figures are given for storm conditions.
Snow: a snow-albedo scheme is used when the current-day snow flag is set (p.3), and snow raises scattered NTL (p.6). Irrelevant for Ian in September; relevant to the Uri stress test (inference).

Encoding quirks (App. B pp.44-45): the offset attribute is named 'offset', not CF 'add_offset' (VNP46A1 uses add_offset, pp.40-43); valid_range is text, e.g. '>=0.0 
' and '0 - 5 
'; units strings end in '
'; the flag layers carry no scale or offset attribute; only DNB_Lunar_Irradiance has a non-unit scale (0.1). The NTL fill is stored as float32 -999.9f, so mask in float32 or with < 0 (the valid range is >= 0), not against a float64 -999.9 after upcasting (inference). Read raw arrays with h5py and mask by hand rather than trusting CF auto-decoding (inference). Format: HDF-EOS5 (HDFEOSVersion 'HDFEOS_5.1.16') in .h5 files (pp.6-7, 45).

lat/lon as printed (pp.43, 45, 50, 58): 1-D float64 arrays of 2400 values, both declared on phony_dim_0. In all four appendices the lon block's attributes are printed with a 'lat:' prefix (lat:valid_min = -180.f, lat:valid_max = 180.f, lat:_FillValue = -999.9f), a documentation artifact to check against a real file. Phony dimension names are assigned by length, so they do not say which axis lon runs along (inference, outside knowledge). Data layers are (phony_dim_0, phony_dim_1) = 2400 × 2400; row orientation is not stated.

QF_Cloud_Mask gaps: the guide does not say bit 0 is the least-significant bit or how multi-bit codes are ordered; bits 14-15, land/water codes 100, 110 and 111, and the meaning of 'VI used' are not described; Table 6 is captioned for VNP46A1 and reaches VNP46A2 by reference (Table 8 footnote 3, p.16). Standard reading (inference): mask the fill 65535 first, then cloud confidence = (qf >> 6) & 3 (0 confident clear, 1 probably clear, 2 probably cloudy, 3 confident cloudy), land/water = (qf >> 1) & 7, and snow/ice = (qf >> 10) & 1.

Corner convention is not stated (corner_convention = null). Tile bounds are whole degrees (h10v04: W -80, E -70, S 40, N 50; pp.39-40, 43-44), which fits outer pixel edges because 2400 × 1/240° = 10° (inference). StructMetadata.0 in 'HDFEOS INFORMATION' is listed but its contents are not shown (p.45). Test on a real h09v06 file (arithmetic): pixel centres give lat[0] ≈ 29.997917, lat[-1] ≈ 20.002083 and lon[0] ≈ -89.997917; top/left edges give 30.0, 20.004167 and -90.0.

Time alignment: the guide gives no overpass time, and per-pixel UTC time exists only in VNP46A1 UTC_Time (pp.12, 43). Outside knowledge, not from the guide: S-NPP's night pass is near 01:30 local mean solar time, which at about 82°W is about UTC-5.5 h, so Lee County passes should fall roughly 06-08 UTC (about 02-04 EDT). The file date is unaffected (2022-09-29 holds the first post-landfall night), but the hour used to match EAGLE-I may need to be 1-2 h later than 01:30 EDT. Check UTC_Time before fixing it.
Lee County tile (derived, not in the guide): h09v06 (90-80°W, 20-30°N) contains all of Lee County (26.3-26.8°N, 81.6-82.3°W).

Latency and archives: daily products are processed within 3-5 h of acquisition (p.2). Standard products are at LAADS DAAC; NRT products come through LANCE with about 3 h latency and serve mainly disaster response (pp.23, 29). VNP46A2 covers January 2012 to present (p.15). The NOAA-20 twin VJ146A2 shares Table 8 (pp.15-16); the guide dates NOAA-20 data (VJ146A1) from January 2018 (p.10).

If VNP46A3/A4 composites serve as a baseline: daily values outside Q1 − 1.5·IQR to Q3 + 1.5·IQR are dropped and the rest averaged (p.5); composite values below 0.5 nW·cm−2·sr−1 are set to zero and aurora pixels are gap-filled (p.6). Composite quality: 0 = good (more than 3 observations), 1 = poor (3 or fewer), 2 = gap filled from historical data, 255 = fill (Table 12 p.23).

Inputs: Table 2 lists VNP46A1, VNP43LGDNBA1, VNPLG09GA and VNP04LGA (p.8). The example VNP46A2.A2024100 InputPointer also lists the same-day VNP46A1, MCD12Q1 (2013) land cover, MODLG44W (a land/water mask, outside knowledge) and an unexplained prior-day VNP46A2_DB.A2024099 file at version .001, and it spells the BRDF input VNPLG43DNBA1 (p.43). The _DB file looks like a rolling store of past values for gap-filling (inference).

Errors in the guide: table cross-references printed without a number (pp.10, 15, 17, 24, 26); Section 5.3 points to List 2 for the A3/A4 contents, which are in List 3 (p.17); 'Equation 4' is cited but only Eqs. 1-3 exist (p.3); two sections are numbered 2.3 (pp.4-5); the List of Tables puts Table 11 on p.15, but it starts on p.18 (p.iv); the Fig. 2 caption says approximately 10°×10° (p.8), while the Fig. 4-6 captions and every metadata bound give exactly 10° (pp.24-26, 39-44, 50, 54).

The guide contains no outage-detection method. Related work it cites: Wang et al. 2018 (disaster power outages, ISPRS archives), Román et al. 2019 (Puerto Rico restoration after Hurricane Maria), Cole et al. 2017, Cao et al. 2013, Molthan & Jedlovec 2013 and Mann et al. 2016 (pp.1, 29-30; reference list pp.31-38).
